intro: You have spent years in this course learning one skill at a time: a twenty-second hand wash, a level cup of flour, a back stitch, a unit price, a food thermometer, a safe crib, a budget built from take-home pay. The capstone asks you to use all of them at once on a single project that you choose, plan, pay for, make, judge and present. It may be a meal for a group or a piece you sew, and it will be yours from the first line of the plan to the last sentence of the presentation.

The first chapter is the plan. You will write a specification that another person could follow, a cost sheet with every ingredient or material at its unit price, a timeline built backwards from the deadline with checkpoints, an equipment list, a safety page with the standard temperatures and rules, and a rubric that says ahead of time what a good result looks like. Every number on those pages is a number you can check.

The second chapter is the doing and the judging. You will run the timeline on production day, record temperatures, times, receipts and photos as you go, serve or finish the piece, and then score it honestly against your own spec and rubric. You will compare plan to actual, name what you would change and why, present the whole project to an audience, and see how the same cycle of plan, cost, produce and evaluate is the daily work of chefs, dietitians, patternmakers, child-care directors and family educators.
bigQuestion: How do you plan, cost, produce and honestly evaluate a real project so that the result is safe, on budget, on time and worth showing?

Ask for more money at the register

test.why: The factor is 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5, and 2 cups × 1.5 = 3 cups.

test.why: Small, necessary supplies are the lines most often forgotten.

test.q: Why does a frozen roast move to the refrigerator days ahead instead of the counter on the day?
choices: Counter thawing leaves the outside in the 40 to 140 °F danger zone for hours
The counter is needed for prep
test.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the whole roast at or below 40 °F.

test.why: Poultry is safe at 165 °F; ground meats at 160 °F; whole cuts of beef and pork at 145 °F with a rest.

test.q: A grease fire starts in a pan on the stove. What does the safety page say?
choices: Smother it with a lid or baking soda, never water
test.why: Water spreads burning grease; a lid or baking soda cuts off the air.

test.why: Only an internal temperature reading is evidence of safety.

test.q: Dinner ended at 8:30; the chicken came out at 5:50. What happens to leftovers?
choices: Discard them; they were out more than two hours
Reheat them to 165 °F and keep them
test.why: The two-hour rule counts from when the food left the oven.

test.q: Which is the strongest reflection statement?

test.why: Action, reason and evidence make a change that a reader can check.

title: Capstone: Plan, Cost, Produce

chapters.title: The Spec and the Cost Sheet
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you turn a big idea into a plan that someone else could pick up and follow?

story.title: Twelve Chairs, Three Courses, One Notebook
story.kicker: A senior offers to cook a real dinner for twelve and discovers that the cooking is the easy part.
paragraphs: Marisol had cooked for her family for years, so when her grandmother's seventieth birthday came around, she said the words before she thought them through: "I'll make the dinner. Three courses. Twelve people." Her aunt raised an eyebrow and asked one question. "What are you serving?" Marisol realized she had no idea.

That night she opened a notebook and wrote the date at the top. Then she stared at the blank page. A soup, maybe. Chicken, because her grandmother liked it. Something sweet. But how much chicken feeds twelve? How many pots did she own? When did the soup need to start if dinner was at six? She did not know a single number yet.

Her FCS teacher had a phrase for this moment. "A wish is not a plan. A plan has numbers, tools and a clock." Marisol started with the guests. Twelve people, one with a shellfish allergy, two who did not eat pork, one small cousin who ate almost nothing. That list changed the menu before she had bought a thing.

By the end of the week the notebook had a menu with quantities, a cost sheet with every item and its price, a list of every pot and pan, and a timeline that started two days before the party. It also had a page called Safety with the food thermometer temperatures written in ink. The dinner was still ten days away, and Marisol already felt like she had done half the work.

She had. In this chapter you will do the same for a project of your own, a meal for a group or a piece of clothing you sew. You will write a specification, cost every part, plan every hour and decide ahead of time what a good result will look like.
story.think: What is one question Marisol should have asked before she offered to cook, and what number would answering it give her?

lessons.title: Pick a Project You Can Finish
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone project is one you can plan, afford, complete on time and evaluate against a clear standard.
reading: Picture two students on the first day of the capstone. One wants to sew a lined wool coat with a zipper and welt pockets. The other wants to make a hemmed apron with two patch pockets. Both are real sewing projects, but only one can be finished in six class periods by a student who has made one drawstring bag. The first step of any project is choosing something that fits the time, the budget, the tools and your own skill.

Use four questions to test an idea. Can I finish it in the time I have? Can I pay for it with the budget I have? Do I have, or can I borrow, every tool it needs? Have I already done the hardest step at least once? If the answer to any question is no, shrink the idea until every answer is yes. A three-course dinner for twelve becomes a two-course dinner for eight. A coat becomes a vest.

Shrinking is not failing. A finished apron with straight seams and even pockets shows more skill than a half-done coat. Employers, judges and teachers all grade the result you deliver, not the one you imagined. Write your idea in one sentence, such as "I will cook a soup, a main dish and a dessert for twelve guests on May 9" or "I will sew a lined tote bag from a commercial pattern by May 9." Every later page of the plan grows from that sentence.

words.d: a final project that pulls together the skills learned across a whole course
the size of a project: what it includes and what it leaves out
a limit you must work within, such as time, money, tools or skill

look.title: Four Ideas, One Choice
look.text: A student has six 50-minute class periods, $30 (example) and access to the school kitchen. Four ideas: (A) a wedding cake with three tiers and fondant; (B) a pan of lasagna and a green salad for ten; (C) a seven-course tasting menu; (D) a batch of handmade croissants, which take two days of folding and chilling.
look.prompt: Which idea passes all four questions, and which single constraint knocks out each of the others?

check.q: A student wants to sew a lined wool coat but has only made one drawstring bag. Which question about the project does this most clearly fail?
choices: Have I done the hardest step before?
Is there a sewing machine available?
check.why: Skill is one of the four tests. A coat's lining, zipper and welt pockets are all steps this student has never done.

check.q: What is the best response when a project idea fails one of the four questions?
choices: Keep the idea and hope for extra time
Shrink the idea until every answer is yes
Ask a friend to do the hard steps
Drop the capstone and do a written report
check.why: Shrinking the scope keeps the project real and finishable. A smaller finished project shows more skill than a large unfinished one.

check.q: Which sentence is a usable one-line project statement?
choices: I want to make something nice for my family
I will cook a great meal sometime this spring
I will sew a lined tote bag from a commercial pattern by May 9
check.why: A project statement names the product, the method and the date. The others leave out the what, the how or the when.

lessons.title: Writing a Specification
lessons.mainIdea: A specification describes the finished product in measurable terms so anyone can tell whether the result meets it.
reading: Imagine handing your plan to a friend who has never seen your project and asking them to make it while you are away. Every question they would have to ask you is a hole in your *specification*. A specification, or spec, is a written description of the finished product: what it is, who it is for, how big it is, what it must do and what it must not contain. Engineers, chefs, tailors and builders all write one before they start.

For a meal, the spec lists the number of guests, the courses, the dishes in each course, the portion size per person, the serving time, and any dietary limits. Example: "Serves 12. Course 1: tomato soup, 1 cup each. Course 2: roast chicken, 6 oz each, with rice and green beans. Course 3: lemon bars, 2 per person. Served at 6:00 p.m. No shellfish. No pork. One child portion at half size." Every line can be checked with a measuring cup, a scale or a clock.

For a sewn piece, the spec names the pattern number and view, the size, the fabric type and yardage, the color, the notions such as thread, zipper and interfacing, the finished measurements, and the seam finish. Example: "Tote bag, pattern view B, 14 by 16 inches finished, medium-weight cotton canvas, lined, 5/8-inch seams pressed open, straps 24 inches long, all seams zigzag finished."

Write in *measurable* terms. "Enough chicken" is not measurable; "6 oz per person, 4.5 lb total" is. "A nice color" is not measurable; "navy blue canvas" is. When you evaluate the project at the end, you will hold the result against this spec line by line, so every line must be something you can see, weigh, measure or time.

words.d: a written, measurable description of what the finished product must be
able to be checked with a tool such as a scale, a ruler, a thermometer or a clock
the amount of one food served to one person
the small sewing supplies a pattern calls for: thread, zippers, buttons, interfacing, elastic

look.title: Find the Holes
look.text: A draft spec reads: "Dinner for my family. Some kind of pasta with sauce, a salad, and dessert. Serve around dinnertime. Make plenty. Watch out for Uncle Ray's allergy." A friend has to cook this without you.
look.prompt: List every question the friend would have to ask, then rewrite the spec so each question is already answered with a number or a name.

check.q: Which line belongs in a specification because it is measurable?
choices: Roast chicken, 6 oz per person, 12 servings
Chicken cooked the way Grandma likes it
check.why: A spec line must be checkable with a tool. Ounces and servings can be weighed and counted; the others cannot.

check.q: A sewing spec should include the fabric yardage. Why?
choices: So the teacher knows you read the pattern
Because it fixes the largest cost and tells you exactly what to buy
Because yardage decides the seam allowance
check.why: Fabric is usually the biggest cost in a sewn project, and the yardage on the pattern envelope tells you the exact amount to purchase.

check.q: A spec says "No shellfish" and "One child portion at half size." What kind of information is this?
choices: Dietary limits and portion rules for specific guests
check.why: The spec records who the meal is for, including allergies, food rules and special portions, so the plan protects each guest.

lessons.title: Know Your Audience
lessons.mainIdea: The people you serve or sew for shape the spec: their number, ages, allergies, food rules, sizes and tastes come before your own preferences.
reading: Marisol's guest list changed her menu before she bought a single ingredient. A shellfish *allergy* meant no shrimp. Two guests who did not eat pork meant chicken, not ham. A small cousin meant a mild dish and a half portion. Your project exists for other people, so the second page of your plan is a plain list of who they are and what they need.

For a meal, gather: the exact head count, any allergies (the nine major allergens are milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame), religious or personal food rules, ages, and anything the host tells you about likes and dislikes. Ask directly and write the answers down. An allergy is a safety matter, not a preference, so an allergen must be kept out of the dish and off the shared cutting board, not just left off the plate.

For a sewn garment, gather the wearer's body measurements taken with a tape over light clothing: bust or chest, waist, hips, back length and any other line the pattern envelope asks for. Compare them to the pattern's size chart and choose the size by the measurements, not by the store size the person usually wears. Ask about fabric feel, color and how the piece will be washed. A shirt for someone who will machine wash it hot should not be cut from a dry-clean-only fabric.

Respect what people tell you. A family that eats no meat on certain days, a guest who fasts, a wearer who wants long sleeves for religious reasons: these are not obstacles to work around but the requirements the spec is built on. The best cooks and tailors are the ones who listen first.

words.d: a food that causes a dangerous immune reaction in some people; nine are named on U.S. labels
the exact number of people who will be served
the table on a pattern envelope that matches body measurements to pattern sizes

look.title: Guest List for the Birthday Dinner (example)
look.prompt: Using these rows, which ingredients must stay out of the whole menu, and how would you size the portions for the child?

check.q: One guest has a peanut allergy. Which plan protects that guest?
choices: Serve the peanut dish but tell the guest which one it is
Leave peanuts out of every dish and keep peanut products off shared boards and utensils
Put the peanuts on the side so they can be skipped
Serve peanuts only in the dessert
check.why: An allergen is a safety hazard. Trace amounts from a shared board or spoon can cause a reaction, so it must be kept out of the kitchen for that meal.

check.q: How should you choose a pattern size for someone you are sewing for?
choices: Use the size they buy in stores
Measure their body and compare to the pattern's size chart
Pick the middle size on the envelope
check.why: Pattern sizes do not match store sizes. The envelope's size chart is keyed to real body measurements.

check.q: A host tells you two guests eat no meat on Fridays and the dinner is on a Friday. What is this information for your plan?
choices: A preference you can ignore if the menu is set
A reason to move the dinner
Something to mention at the table
A requirement the spec must be built around
check.why: Food rules from faith or personal choice are requirements of the project, recorded in the spec and honored in the menu.

lessons.title: Every Ingredient, Every Material
lessons.mainIdea: A cost sheet lists every single item the project uses, with its unit price and the amount needed, so the total is real and not a guess.
reading: Look at Marisol's first cost estimate: "Chicken, rice, beans, soup stuff, dessert stuff: about $60." Now look at her second: twenty-three lines, each with an item, a package size, a package price, the amount she actually needs and the cost of that amount. The first number was a wish. The second was a *cost sheet*. The difference was two hours in a grocery store aisle with her phone and a notebook.

Build the sheet from the recipes, not from memory. Open each recipe, scaled to your head count, and copy every ingredient down, including the ones that seem too small to matter: salt, oil, the parchment paper, the foil. For a sewing project, copy every line from the pattern envelope's back: fabric, lining, interfacing, thread, zipper, buttons, and add the things the envelope does not list, such as a new machine needle or a marking pen.

Give the sheet five columns: item, package size and price, unit price, amount needed, and cost of the amount needed. Unit price is the package price divided by the package size. Example: a 5-lb bag of rice at $4.50 (example) is $0.90 per lb. If the recipe needs 3 lb, the cost line is 3 × $0.90 = $2.70. Do this for every line, then add the column. That sum is your ingredient or material cost.

Forgetting a line is the most common mistake, and the forgotten line is usually a cheap one that turns into a trip to the store on the day of the event. The second most common mistake is copying the package price into the cost column when you only use part of the package. You will still have to buy the whole package, so keep a sixth column for what you will actually spend at the register.

words.d: a table listing every item a project uses, its unit price, the amount needed and the resulting cost
the price of one unit of an item, found by dividing the package price by the package size
one row on a cost sheet: a single ingredient or material

look.title: Unit Prices From the Store Shelf (example)
look.cite: example prices for practice; real prices vary by store and season
look.prompt: The chicken course needs 4.5 lb of thighs, 3 lb of rice and 3 lb of green beans. Compute each cost line and the total for the course.

check.q: A 5-lb bag of rice costs $4.50 (example). The recipe needs 3 lb. What goes in the cost column?
check.why: Unit price is $4.50 ÷ 5 = $0.90 per lb, and 3 lb × $0.90 = $2.70.

check.q: Where should the list of ingredients on a cost sheet come from?
choices: Memory of what is usually in the dish
The scaled recipe, line by line
check.why: Copying from the scaled recipe catches every ingredient, including small ones like salt, oil and parchment that memory skips.

check.q: Why keep a separate column for the register total when a recipe uses only part of a package?
choices: Because you still have to buy the whole package
Because sales tax is added later
Because the unit price is only an estimate
Because leftovers must be thrown out
check.why: The cost column shows what the project consumes; the register column shows the cash you must have, since stores sell whole packages.

lessons.title: Scaling Recipes to the Head Count
lessons.mainIdea: To scale a recipe, divide the servings you need by the servings it makes to get a factor, then multiply every ingredient by that factor and convert to sensible units.
reading: Marisol's lemon bar recipe makes 12 bars in an 8-by-8-inch pan. Her spec says 2 bars each for 12 people, which is 24 bars. The *scaling factor* is 24 ÷ 12 = 2. Every ingredient is multiplied by 2: 1 cup of flour becomes 2 cups, ½ cup of butter becomes 1 cup, 3 eggs become 6, 2 Tbsp of lemon juice become 4 Tbsp, which is ¼ cup. Two 8-by-8 pans, or one 9-by-13, hold the doubled batch.

Factors are not always whole numbers. A soup recipe that serves 8 must serve 12, so the factor is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5. If the soup calls for 4 cups of broth, the scaled amount is 6 cups, which is 1.5 quarts. If it calls for 1 Tbsp of oil, you need 1.5 Tbsp, which is 1 Tbsp plus 1.5 tsp, since 3 tsp make 1 Tbsp. Write the scaled amount in the unit you can actually measure.

Some things do not scale in a straight line. Cooking time rises for a larger pot but not by the factor; a doubled roast does not take twice as long, so you cook by internal temperature and a thermometer, never by the clock alone. Seasonings like salt and hot pepper are usually scaled by the factor and then tasted and adjusted. Pan size must be checked separately, because a doubled cake batter in the original pan overflows.

Compute every scaled line twice, once when you write it and once the next day, and mark the sheet with the check. A single arithmetic slip, such as writing 2 tsp when you meant 2 Tbsp, is a small mistake on paper and a ruined dish in the pan, and it is the kind of error a second look always catches.

words.d: the number you multiply each ingredient by: servings needed divided by servings the recipe makes
how much a recipe makes, in servings or pieces
the temperature at the center of a food, read with a food thermometer

look.title: Scale the Soup
look.text: Tomato soup, serves 8: 2 Tbsp olive oil, 1 onion, 2 cans (28 oz each) crushed tomatoes, 4 cups broth, 1 tsp salt, ½ cup cream. The spec needs 12 servings of 1 cup each.
look.prompt: Find the factor, rewrite every line in a unit you can measure, and state which line you would taste and adjust rather than trust the math.

check.q: A recipe serves 8 and you need 12 servings. What is the scaling factor?
check.why: Servings needed ÷ servings the recipe makes = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5.

check.q: A recipe calls for 2 Tbsp lemon juice and the factor is 2. Which is the scaled amount written in a measurable unit?
check.why: 2 Tbsp × 2 = 4 Tbsp, and 4 Tbsp = ¼ cup.

check.q: You double a chicken recipe. How should you decide when the chicken is done?
choices: Read 165 °F at the thickest part with a food thermometer
Cook until the outside is brown
check.why: Cooking time does not scale by the factor. Poultry is done at a safe minimum internal temperature of 165 °F, checked with a thermometer.

lessons.title: Hidden Costs and the Budget Line
lessons.mainIdea: Beyond ingredients or fabric, a real cost sheet includes supplies, equipment you must buy or rent, a waste allowance and a cushion, compared against the budget you were given.
reading: A student sewing a tote bag priced the canvas, lining, thread and webbing and came to $18.40 (example). Then the machine needle broke on the first seam, the interfacing was not on the sheet, and the bag needed a magnetic snap the pattern had listed in tiny print. The real total was $27.10. Nothing on the second list was expensive, but together they were almost half again the first number. These are *hidden costs*, and the cost sheet needs a section for them.

Add a block below the ingredient or material lines. For a meal: foil, parchment, storage containers for leftovers, dish soap, disposable plates or napkins if used, ice, and any equipment you must buy, rent or borrow such as a large stockpot or a second roasting pan. For a sewn piece: needles, marking tools, interfacing, fusible tape, pattern cost, and a pressing cloth. Price each one the same way, unit price times amount.

Then add two lines that are not things at all. The first is a waste allowance, because peeling, trimming and cutting on grain all lose material. Cooks often buy about 10 percent more produce than the recipe weight; sewers buy the envelope's yardage, which already includes layout waste, but add fabric for a matched print or a cutting mistake. The second is a cushion, a small amount, often 5 to 10 percent of the total, held back for a price that rose or an item you forgot.

Finally, write the *budget* line: the money you actually have. Compare the total to it. If the total is higher, change the plan now, not at the register. Swap a store brand for a name brand, choose chicken thighs over breasts, replace fresh berries with frozen, drop the lining or pick a less costly fabric. The spec may change slightly; the budget does not.

words.d: a small necessary expense that is easy to forget, such as foil, needles or interfacing
extra material bought because trimming, peeling and cutting lose some of it
money held back in a budget for a price change or a forgotten item
the amount of money you have to spend on the whole project

look.title: Tote Bag Cost Sheet, Two Versions (example)
look.prompt: Confirm the real total by adding the four hidden lines to the first estimate, then say what a 10 percent cushion on the real total would be.

check.q: A meal's ingredient total is $80 (example). What would a 10 percent cushion be?
check.why: 10 percent of $80 is $8, held back for a price rise or a forgotten item.

check.q: Which item is a hidden cost most students forget on a sewing cost sheet?
choices: Interfacing listed in small print on the envelope
check.why: Interfacing, needles and snaps are small, necessary and easy to overlook. The main fabric is never forgotten.

check.q: The cost total comes to $95 and the budget is $80 (example). What is the right move?
choices: Buy everything and hope for a sale
Change the plan now, such as store brands or a cheaper cut, until the total fits
Skip the cushion and the waste allowance
check.why: The budget is the fixed constraint. The plan is adjusted before shopping, not at the register.

lessons.title: Working Backwards From the Deadline
lessons.mainIdea: Build the timeline from the finish time backwards, giving each task its real duration, so that the longest and earliest jobs start first.
reading: Dinner is at 6:00 p.m. A roast chicken takes about 1 hour 30 minutes in the oven plus 15 minutes of rest, so it goes in at 4:15. The oven must preheat, so it is turned on at 4:00. The chicken must be seasoned before that, at 3:45. Read those times again: they were found by starting at the end and stepping backwards. That is how every timeline for a project is built.

List every task the project needs, including the ones that are not cooking or sewing: shopping, washing produce, thawing, preheating, pressing fabric, cutting, resting, cooling, plating, cleanup. Next to each, write how long it really takes, timed from experience or from the recipe or pattern, not from hope. Then place the last task at the deadline and work backwards, task by task, until you reach the first thing you must do.

Thawing is the task most often placed wrong. A 4-to-5-lb chicken thaws in the refrigerator in about a day, so it moves from freezer to fridge two days before the dinner to be safe. It never thaws on the counter, because the outside sits in the danger zone of 40 to 140 °F while the inside is still frozen. Dessert that must cool and set, such as lemon bars, is baked the day before. Fabric is washed, dried and pressed the day before cutting.

Mark *checkpoints*: a few moments where you stop and confirm that you are on schedule. "Day before, 8 p.m.: dessert baked and chilled, chicken thawed, all produce washed. Day of, 3:30: soup simmering, oven on at 4:00." A missed checkpoint tells you early enough to fix it, by simplifying a dish or asking for help, instead of at 5:55 with twelve people at the table.

words.d: a schedule that lists every task with its start time, built backwards from the deadline
a set moment in the timeline where you confirm the work is on schedule
40 to 140 °F, the temperature range where bacteria in food multiply fastest

look.title: Put the Evening in Order
look.text: Dinner at 6:00. Tasks with real durations: rest the chicken 15 min; roast 90 min; preheat oven 15 min; season chicken 10 min; cook rice 25 min; steam green beans 8 min; reheat soup 15 min; set the table 10 min. Only one person is cooking.
look.prompt: Write the start time for each task working backwards from 6:00, and name which tasks can overlap while the chicken roasts.

check.q: A chicken needs 90 minutes to roast and 15 minutes to rest, and dinner is at 6:00. When does it go in the oven?
check.why: Work backwards: 6:00 minus 15 minutes rest is 5:45, minus 90 minutes roasting is 4:15.

check.q: Why must a frozen chicken be moved to the refrigerator two days before the dinner?
choices: Because the freezer must be emptied
Because a large bird takes about a day to thaw in the fridge, and counter thawing leaves it in the danger zone
check.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the whole bird at or below 40 °F. A counter lets the outside sit between 40 and 140 °F for hours.

check.q: What is the purpose of a checkpoint in the timeline?
choices: To record the cost of each task
To catch a delay early enough to fix it
check.why: A checkpoint compares the plan to the clock while there is still time to simplify or get help.

lessons.title: The Materials and Equipment List
lessons.mainIdea: List every tool and piece of equipment for every step, check that you have it or can borrow it, and stage it before you start.
reading: Marisol's soup recipe said "blend until smooth." She did not own a blender. She found this out at 3:40 p.m. on the day of the party, with a pot of hot chunky soup in front of her. A tool list would have caught it a week earlier. For each step in the recipe or pattern, write the tool that step needs, then walk through your kitchen or sewing room and check each one off.

Group the list by station. For a meal: prep (cutting boards, one for raw meat and one for produce, a chef's knife, a paring knife, peeler, measuring cups and spoons, bowls), cooking (pots by size, roasting pan, sheet pans, tongs, spatula, whisk, food thermometer), serving (platters, ladle, serving spoons, twelve of every plate, bowl and glass), and storage (containers with lids, foil, labels). For sewing: cutting (shears, rotary cutter and mat, pins, weights), marking (chalk, tracing paper), sewing (machine, correct needle, bobbins, seam ripper), pressing (iron, board, pressing cloth), and finishing (hand needles, tape measure).

Count the ones that matter. Twelve guests need twelve bowls and twelve spoons, plus serving pieces. A three-course dinner may need more pots on the stove than you have burners, which changes the timeline, not just the list. If something is missing, decide now: borrow it, buy it and add it to the cost sheet, or change the method. Soup can be left chunky; a potato masher stands in for a blender.

The day before, stage the equipment: pull it out, wash it, and set it where it will be used. A thermometer that lives in a drawer gets forgotten; one sitting beside the stove gets used. This is *mise en place* for tools, the same idea as measuring ingredients before you cook, and it is the single habit that most separates a calm cook from a frantic one.

words.d: every tool, pan, machine and serving piece a project needs, checked against what you have
one area of a kitchen or workroom set up for one kind of task, such as prep or pressing
French for everything in its place: tools and ingredients ready before work starts
a probe thermometer that reads the internal temperature of food

look.title: Walk the Recipe for Tools
look.text: Recipe steps: (1) dice 2 onions and mince 4 garlic cloves; (2) sauté in a 6-quart pot; (3) add tomatoes and broth, simmer 25 min; (4) blend until smooth; (5) stir in cream, taste; (6) ladle 1 cup into each of 12 bowls. The kitchen has a 4-quart pot, one cutting board, a chef's knife, a wooden spoon and a potato masher.
look.prompt: Name the tool each step needs, mark which ones are missing, and decide for each missing one whether to borrow, buy or change the method.

check.q: Why should raw chicken and salad greens be cut on separate boards?
choices: To prevent cross-contamination of ready-to-eat food with raw-meat bacteria
check.why: Raw poultry juices carry bacteria that cooking would kill in the chicken but that would survive on uncooked greens.

check.q: A three-course dinner needs five pots at once and the stove has four burners. What does this change?
choices: The timeline, since some dishes must cook earlier and be held or reheated
check.why: Equipment limits shape the schedule. A dish cooked ahead is reheated to 165 °F when it is time to serve.

check.q: What does it mean to stage equipment?
choices: Buy it new for the event
Pull it out, wash it and set it where it will be used before starting
check.why: Staging is mise en place for tools: a thermometer beside the stove gets used, one in a drawer gets forgotten.

lessons.title: The Safety Plan
lessons.mainIdea: A safety plan writes down the standard temperatures, times and rules for the project before the day, so that safety decisions are already made.
reading: At 5:30 on the day of the dinner, with the soup boiling and the guests arriving, nobody remembers whether chicken is 160 or 165 °F. So the number is written on a page taped to the cabinet a week earlier. A *safety plan* is that page: every safety figure and rule the project depends on, decided in a calm moment and posted where the work happens.

For a meal, the page holds the standard figures. Safe minimum internal temperatures: poultry 165 °F; ground meats 160 °F; whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal 145 °F with a 3-minute rest; fish 145 °F; leftovers reheated to 165 °F; eggs cooked until firm. Cold food is held at or below 40 °F and the freezer at 0 °F. The two-hour rule: perishable food that has sat out for more than two hours, or one hour above 90 °F, is discarded. Hands are washed for 20 seconds before starting, after touching raw meat, and after any interruption. Raw meat gets its own board. A lid and baking soda sit near the stove for a grease fire, and water never goes on one.

For a sewing project, the page covers the machine and the iron. Fingers stay clear of the needle; the foot is off the pedal while threading; pins are removed before the needle reaches them, never sewn over. The iron is set to the fabric's setting, rests on its heel, is never left face down, and is unplugged when the session ends. Shears and rotary blades are closed or capped when set down and carried point down. Long hair is tied back around both the machine and the stove.

Add the allergen line from your audience list to the safety page in large letters, with the rule that the allergen does not enter the kitchen during the project. Add the emergency numbers and the location of the first-aid kit and fire extinguisher. Then sign and date the page. When you evaluate the project, this page is one of the things you will be graded on, and it is the one page where "almost right" is not a passing grade.

words.d: a written page of the standard temperatures, times and rules a project depends on, posted where the work happens
perishable food left out more than two hours, or one hour above 90 °F, must be thrown away
the spread of bacteria from one food or surface to another, such as raw chicken juice onto salad

look.title: Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures
rows: beef, pork, lamb, veal whole cuts, plus 3-min rest
look.cite: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, safe minimum internal temperature chart
look.prompt: Which of these figures belong on Marisol's posted safety page for a menu of tomato soup, roast chicken and lemon bars, and where in the timeline will each be checked?

check.q: The roast chicken thermometer reads 150 °F at the thickest part of the thigh. What does the safety plan say?
choices: Serve it; the outside is brown
Serve it and reheat leftovers later
check.why: Poultry's safe minimum internal temperature is 165 °F. The 145 °F with rest rule applies to whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal, not chicken.

check.q: The soup was made the day before. How hot must it be when reheated for serving?
check.why: Leftovers are reheated to an internal temperature of 165 °F.

check.q: Which sewing rule belongs on the safety page?
choices: Sew slowly over pins so they do not fall out
Leave the iron face down so it stays hot
Thread the machine with the pedal ready
Remove pins before the needle reaches them and keep the foot off the pedal while threading
check.why: Sewing over pins can break the needle and send a fragment flying; threading with the foot on the pedal risks a stitched finger.

lessons.title: Writing the Rubric First
lessons.mainIdea: A rubric written before the work names what a good result looks like at each level, so the finished project can be judged fairly against the spec.
reading: Ask a friend to taste your soup and they will say "good." Ask them to score it on a *rubric* and they will tell you the salt was right, the texture was slightly grainy and the portion was exactly one cup. A rubric is a table: the rows are the things that matter, and the columns describe what each row looks like at levels such as excellent, good, needs work and not met. Writing it before the project turns the spec into a scoring tool.

Choose the rows from the spec. For a meal, common rows are: served on time, portion size matches the spec, food safety figures met and recorded, taste and seasoning, texture and doneness, appearance and plating, cost within budget, cleanup complete. For a sewn piece: fits the spec's measurements, seams straight and at 5/8 inch, seam finish as specified, pressing, topstitching even, notions attached securely, cost within budget, finished on time.

Describe each level in words that can be checked. For "served on time": excellent means every course within 5 minutes of the plan; good means within 15 minutes; needs work means one course more than 15 minutes late; not met means a course was not served. For "seams": excellent means every seam at 5/8 inch within 1/16 inch and no puckers; good means one seam off by 1/8 inch; and so on. Numbers make the rubric fair to you and to the judge.

Give each row a weight. Safety and the spec's required items weigh most; appearance weighs less. Then, before you begin, score the plan itself: a plan with no thermometer check in the timeline cannot score excellent on safety. Fix the plan, not the rubric. On the day the project is evaluated, you and your teacher will each fill in the same table, and the conversation about where the scores differ is where the real learning happens.

words.d: a scoring table whose rows are the things that matter and whose columns describe each level of quality
one row of a rubric: a single thing the result is judged on
how much one rubric row counts toward the total score

look.title: Fix the Vague Rubric
look.text: A draft rubric row for a tote bag reads: Seams. Excellent: really good seams. Good: pretty good seams. Needs work: seams are a little off. Not met: bad seams. The spec called for 5/8-inch seams, pressed open, zigzag finished.
look.prompt: Rewrite the four levels so each can be checked with a seam gauge and your eyes, then give the row a weight and explain why.

check.q: When should the rubric for a capstone project be written?
choices: Before the work starts, from the spec
check.why: A rubric written first turns the spec into a scoring tool and shapes the plan; written afterwards, it just describes what happened.

check.q: Which rubric level description is checkable?
choices: Excellent: every course served within 5 minutes of the planned time
check.why: A checkable level uses a number or a tool. Minutes on a clock can be verified; delicious cannot.

check.q: A plan has no thermometer check anywhere on the timeline. What should change?
choices: The rubric, to drop the safety row
The weight of the appearance row
The plan, to add the temperature check at the right time
check.why: The plan is fixed to meet the rubric, never the reverse. Safety rows carry the most weight and must be met.

review.q: A student has six class periods and $30 (example). Which project fits the constraints?
review.why: Lasagna and salad can be planned, afforded and finished in the time; each of the others fails time, cost or skill.

review.q: Which line is written the way a specification requires?
choices: Tote bag, 14 by 16 inches finished, cotton canvas, 5/8-inch seams
A bag big enough for books
A bag like the one in the store
review.why: Specs use measurable terms: dimensions, fabric type and seam allowance can all be checked.

review.q: A 5-lb bag of flour costs $3.00 (example). What is the unit price per pound?
review.why: Package price divided by package size: $3.00 ÷ 5 lb = $0.60 per lb.

review.q: A cookie recipe yields 24 cookies and you need 36. What is the scaling factor?
review.why: 36 ÷ 24 = 1.5, and every ingredient is multiplied by 1.5.

review.q: Dinner is at 7:00. A dish takes 40 minutes to bake and 10 minutes to rest. When does it go in the oven?
review.why: 7:00 minus 10 minutes rest is 6:50, minus 40 minutes baking is 6:10.

review.q: A frozen turkey breast is needed Saturday at 4 p.m. Which thawing plan is safe?
choices: In a sink of warm water Saturday noon
review.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the meat at or below 40 °F the whole time; the counter and warm water leave it in the danger zone.

review.q: Ground beef for the sliders reads 150 °F. What is the safe minimum internal temperature for ground meats?
review.why: Ground meats are safe at 160 °F; 145 °F with a rest applies to whole cuts, and 165 °F to poultry and leftovers.

review.q: What is the purpose of giving a rubric row a weight?
choices: To show how much that criterion counts toward the total, with safety counting most
To make the table look complete
To lower the score of a difficult project
review.why: Weights rank the criteria. Safety and required spec items carry the most weight; appearance carries less.

chapters.title: Making, Evaluating and Presenting
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you carry a plan through to a finished result, judge it honestly and show your work to others?

story.title: Six O'Clock, and the Scoring Begins
story.kicker: The dinner goes onto the table, and the hardest part of the project turns out to be telling the truth about it.
paragraphs: At 5:52 p.m. Marisol pulled the thermometer from the thickest part of the chicken thigh and read 167 °F. She wrote the number and the time on the safety page taped to the cabinet, set the pan on the counter to rest, and started the timer for fifteen minutes. The soup was already at 165 °F on the back burner. The lemon bars had been cut that morning. Her phone, propped against the flour canister, had a photo of every step since Thursday.

The soup went out at 6:04, four minutes behind the plan. The chicken went out at 6:31. The rice, which she had cooked early and held in the oven, had dried a little at the edges. Her grandmother said it was the best dinner she had ever eaten, which was kind and, Marisol knew, not a rubric score.

The next day she sat down with her spec, her cost sheet, her timeline and the rubric she had written two weeks before. Served on time: soup within five minutes, excellent; chicken within fifteen, good. Portion size: one cup of soup, six ounces of chicken, met. Safety: every temperature recorded, met. Texture: rice dry at the edges, needs work. Cost: $87.40 against an $85 budget (example), over by $2.40.

Her teacher read the sheet and asked one question. "What would you change?" Marisol had an answer ready, because she had written it the night of the dinner while it was fresh: cook the rice last, not first, and buy the chicken at the store where it was $0.30 a pound cheaper. That answer, more than the chicken, was what the capstone was for.

In this chapter you will produce your own project on schedule, document it as you go, score it honestly against the spec and the rubric, and present it to an audience. Then you will look at the careers where people do exactly this work for a living.
story.think: Marisol's grandmother said it was the best dinner ever. Why is that not enough for the evaluation, and what did the rubric catch that the compliment did not?

lessons.title: Running the Timeline
lessons.mainIdea: On the production day you follow the timeline you wrote, check the clock at every checkpoint and adjust the plan, not the safety rules, when you fall behind.
reading: It is the morning of the project. The timeline is taped beside the safety page. The first task on it is not cooking; it is a five-minute walk through the plan: read every line, confirm every ingredient is in the kitchen, every tool is staged, and the thermometer has a battery. Then wash your hands for 20 seconds, tie back your hair, and start the first task at the time written next to it, not earlier and not later.

Work from the paper, not from memory. Cross off each task as it finishes and write the actual time beside the planned one. At each *checkpoint*, stop for thirty seconds and compare. If you are ahead, do not start the next hot task early; use the time to clean or to prep the next step's ingredients. If you are behind, decide what to cut, and cut the least important thing. A garnish goes before a course; a second side dish goes before the main; nothing on the safety page ever goes.

Common day-of mistakes come from skipping the paper. A student who "knows the recipe" forgets the salt; one who starts the rice first because it is easy serves it dry; one who does not write the thermometer reading cannot prove the chicken was safe. Another common mistake is doing every task in series when the timeline planned overlaps: while the chicken roasts for 90 minutes, the beans are trimmed, the table is set and the soup is reheated. The oven does the work; you do the next task.

For a sewing project the same rules hold. The timeline says press, cut, mark, sew in order, and the checkpoints fall after cutting and after the first major seam. If the first seam is off, you find it at the checkpoint with a seam gauge and rip it while it is one seam, not after the lining is in. Keep the *seam ripper* on the table, not in the box: using it early is a sign of a careful worker, not a failed one.

words.d: the day the project is actually cooked or sewn, following the timeline
a planned moment to compare actual progress to the timeline
a small hooked blade for cutting stitches to remove a seam
doing one task while another, such as roasting, runs on its own

look.title: Behind at the 4:30 Checkpoint
look.text: The 4:30 checkpoint says: chicken in the oven, soup reheating, beans trimmed, table set. It is 4:30 and the chicken went in at 4:25, the soup is still in the fridge, the beans are untrimmed, and the table is bare. Dinner is at 6:00. The plan also had a garnish of fried shallots for the soup.
look.prompt: Decide what to cut, what to overlap and what must stay unchanged, and write the new order of tasks from 4:30 to 6:00.

check.q: You reach a checkpoint 20 minutes behind. Which is the right thing to cut first?
choices: The thermometer check on the chicken
The fried shallot garnish for the soup
The hand washing after handling raw meat
check.why: Cut the least important item. Garnish goes before a course; nothing on the safety page is ever cut.

check.q: Why write the actual time beside each planned time as you work?
choices: So the evaluation can compare plan to reality and improve the next timeline
So guests know when to arrive
check.why: Recorded times are the data for honest evaluation and for a better plan next time.

check.q: The chicken roasts for 90 minutes. What should the cook be doing during that time?
choices: Opening the oven every ten minutes to check
Overlapping tasks: trimming beans, setting the table, reheating soup
check.why: The timeline plans overlaps so that the oven's time is also the cook's time for other tasks.

lessons.title: Documenting as You Go
lessons.mainIdea: Photos, times, temperatures and short notes taken during the work are the evidence you will need to evaluate the project and present it.
reading: At the evaluation Marisol could say "the chicken reached 167 °F at 5:52" because she wrote it down at 5:52. She could show the mise en place on Thursday, the cost sheet with receipts stapled to it, the chicken going into the oven, and the plated soup. None of that could have been reconstructed the next day from memory. *Documentation* is recorded while it happens or not at all.

Keep three kinds of records. First, numbers: every thermometer reading with its time, the actual start and finish time of each task, the register total from each receipt, the finished measurements of a sewn piece. Second, photos: the staged tools, each major step, each finished component, the final plate or garment from the front and back, and any problem, such as a puckered seam or a scorched pan, exactly as it looked. Third, short notes: one line when something goes differently from the plan, written in the moment. "4:41 rice done too early, holding in oven."

Set up documentation before the work so it does not slow the work. A phone on a stand at the counter, a pencil tied to the timeline, a folder for receipts. Wash your hands after touching the phone and before touching food again, and keep the phone off the prep surface; it is one of the dirtiest objects in the room. Take the photo, then wash, then continue.

Photograph problems as carefully as successes. The judge will believe a report that shows the dry rice more than one that shows only the good plates, and the dry rice is the part you learn from. A sewing student who photographs the first crooked seam beside the ripped and resewn one has shown more skill than one who shows only the finished bag.

words.d: the numbers, photos and notes recorded during a project as evidence of what happened
the store's printed record of what you bought and paid, kept for the cost sheet
records that prove a claim, such as a written thermometer reading with its time

look.title: What Would You Have Recorded?
look.text: A student's project report says: "The chicken was cooked all the way. The dinner was mostly on time. I spent about what I planned. The lemon bars were great and everyone liked them." There are two photos, both of the finished table.
look.prompt: For each sentence, name the number, photo or note that would turn it into evidence, and say when during the day it had to be taken.

check.q: Which record proves the chicken was safe to serve?
choices: A written thermometer reading of 165 °F or higher with the time it was taken
A photo of the browned skin
check.why: Only an internal temperature reading is evidence of safety; color and time are not.

check.q: Why should the phone stay off the prep surface and hands be washed after using it?
choices: Phones carry many bacteria and can contaminate food and surfaces
The teacher does not allow phones
check.why: A phone is handled constantly and is one of the dirtiest objects in a kitchen, so it is treated like any other contaminated item.

check.q: Why photograph a problem such as a scorched pan or a puckered seam?
choices: To prove the project was hard
So the evaluation is honest and the problem can be analyzed and fixed next time
Because the rubric requires ten photos
check.why: Problems are the part you learn from, and a report that shows them earns more trust than one that hides them.

lessons.title: Serving and Finishing
lessons.mainIdea: The final steps of plating and serving, or pressing and finishing, decide how the work is received, and they follow rules of temperature, timing and care like every earlier step.
reading: Twelve bowls of soup do not fill themselves. Marisol laid out twelve warmed bowls on the counter in a grid, ladled one level cup into each, wiped each rim with a clean towel, and carried them out three at a time. Hot food is served hot: above 140 °F, out of the danger zone, on warm plates. Cold food is served cold, at or below 40 °F, so the salad stayed in the refrigerator until the moment it went out. Serving is the last cooking step, and it has the same rules.

Plate in an order. The main item goes down first, in the same spot on every plate; sides go beside it; sauce goes over or under, never dripped across the rim; garnish goes on last and only if it is edible and belongs to the dish. Wipe the rim. Check every plate against the spec's portion before it leaves the counter: a scale or a measuring cup at the plating station keeps six ounces from becoming four on the last plate. Serve everyone at a table at the same time, then clear the course before the next one comes.

For a sewn piece, finishing is pressing, trimming and checking. Every seam is pressed as sewn, then open or to one side as the pattern says. Threads are clipped. Notions are tested: the snap closes, the zipper runs, the buttons hold. The piece is measured against the spec's finished measurements, and any marking chalk is brushed away. A garment is tried on the person it was made for, and the fit is noted for the evaluation.

Cleanup is part of finishing, not something after it. Leftovers go into shallow containers, labeled with the date, and into the refrigerator within two hours of cooking. The stove, boards and counters are washed and sanitized, the thermometer is wiped and put back, and the machine is covered and the iron unplugged. The rubric has a row for this, and it is the row most often lost by a project that was otherwise excellent.

words.d: arranging food on a plate in a set order and checking portion and rim before serving
hot food kept above 140 °F and cold food at or below 40 °F until served
an edible addition placed on a finished dish for appearance and flavor
the dimensions of a completed sewn piece, compared to the spec

look.title: Holding and Serving Figures
rows: cold food held at or below
look.cite: USDA and FDA food-safety guidance, standard figures
look.prompt: Marisol's rice came out of the pot at 4:41 and dinner was at 6:00. Using these rows, explain how it should have been held and what the alternative was.

check.q: Soup finished at 5:30 must be served at 6:15. How should it be held?
choices: In the pot on the counter with the lid on
Above 140 °F on a low burner or in a warm oven
In the refrigerator, then served as is
On the table so it cools to eating temperature
check.why: Hot food is held above 140 °F, above the danger zone, until it is served.

check.q: The dinner ends at 8:30 and the chicken came out of the oven at 5:52. What happens to the leftovers?
choices: Leave them on the counter to cool overnight
They were out more than two hours and must be discarded
check.why: The two-hour rule counts from when the food came out of the oven. Food out longer than two hours is thrown away.

check.q: Which is the correct order for plating?
choices: Sauce on the rim, then main
Sides first, then main on top
Main in the same spot on every plate, sides beside, sauce, garnish last, wipe the rim
check.why: A set order gives every plate the same look, and the rim wipe is the last step before the plate leaves the counter.

lessons.title: Scoring Against the Spec
lessons.mainIdea: Evaluation means putting the finished result beside the spec and the rubric line by line and recording what met, what did not and by how much.
reading: Lay the spec on the left and your documentation on the right. Read the first line of the spec: "Serves 12." Did it? Twelve bowls, twelve plates, twelve desserts: met. Next line: "Soup, 1 cup each." The ladle was a one-cup ladle and each bowl got one level scoop: met. Next: "Chicken, 6 oz each." The scale at the plating station read between 5.5 and 6.5 oz: met within a reasonable range. Go line by line to the end, and write met, not met or partly met beside each.

Then open the rubric and score each row using the evidence, not your feelings. "Served on time" is scored from the actual times written on the timeline. "Safety" is scored from the recorded temperatures. "Cost within budget" is scored from the receipts against the budget line. "Texture and doneness" is scored from tasting notes and photos, and here you must be the harshest taster at the table: the rice was dry at the edges, and dry is a texture fault, so the row is needs work even though nobody complained.

For a sewn piece, score with tools. A seam gauge on every seam; a tape measure on the finished dimensions; a close look at the stitching on both sides under good light; the closure tested ten times. Compare to the rubric levels you wrote, which used numbers such as 5/8 inch within 1/16, so there is no argument about what excellent means.

Total the weighted score and write it down before you talk to anyone. Then compare with your teacher's scoring of the same table. Where the two scores agree, you have learned to see your own work clearly. Where they differ, ask why, and look at the evidence together. Honest self-evaluation is the skill employers describe when they say someone "takes feedback well."

words.d: judging a finished result against the spec and the rubric using evidence
scoring your own work honestly before anyone else does
a small ruler with a slider used to check seam allowance and hem depth

look.title: Marisol's Rubric Scores (example, out of 4)
look.prompt: Multiply each score by its weight, total the points, and compute the maximum possible. Which two rows cost the most points, and which one was fully in Marisol's control?

check.q: The spec says 6 oz of chicken per person. How is this line evaluated?
choices: By asking guests whether they were full
By checking the recipe's serving count
By the scale readings taken at the plating station
By the weight of the raw chicken
check.why: A measurable spec line is checked with the tool named, and the plating-station scale readings are the evidence.

check.q: Nobody complained about the dry rice. How should the texture row be scored?
choices: Good, because it was only the edges
Not scored, because it was a side dish
Needs work, because dry rice is a texture fault the evidence shows
check.why: Rows are scored from evidence against the rubric's own levels, not from compliments.

check.q: Why score your own project before hearing the teacher's score?
choices: To learn to see your own work clearly and then compare where the two differ
To argue for a higher grade
Because the teacher does not score it
check.why: Self-evaluation is a skill. Comparing two independent scores shows where your judgment is accurate and where it is not.

lessons.title: Cost and Time, Plan Against Actual
lessons.mainIdea: Compare the planned cost sheet and timeline with what really happened, find every difference and name its cause.
reading: Marisol's cost sheet planned $85.00 and the receipts totaled $87.40 (example). Two dollars and forty cents over is small, but the useful question is not how much; it is where. She laid the receipts beside the sheet. Chicken: planned $2.49 per lb, paid $2.79, because the sale had ended; on 4.5 lb that was $1.35 more. Lemons: planned 6 at $0.50, bought 8 because two were soft, $1.00 more. Foil: not on the sheet at all, $0.05 short of her cushion covering it. The total told her she was over; the lines told her why.

Do the same with time. Beside each planned time on the timeline is the actual time you wrote on the day. Subtract. The soup went out 4 minutes late because the bowls were not warmed until 5:55. The chicken went out 16 minutes late because the rest ran long while the soup was cleared. The rice was done 79 minutes early because it was started first. Each *variance* has a cause, and the cause is what gets fixed next time.

Sort the causes into three kinds. Things outside your control, such as a sale that ended: you cannot prevent them, but you can plan for them with a cushion, which is exactly what the cushion is for. Things in the plan, such as starting the rice first: the plan was wrong and is rewritten. Things in the execution, such as forgetting to warm the bowls: the plan was right and was not followed, so the fix is a line on the timeline or a checkpoint that catches it.

Write the comparison as a short table with four columns: item, planned, actual, cause. Keep it to the lines that differed. Then write one sentence for money and one for time: "Over budget by $2.40 (example), mostly from the chicken price; covered by the cushion. Main course 16 minutes late, from an unplanned overlap between the rest and clearing." Those two sentences, backed by the table, are the core of the presentation.

words.d: the difference between a planned figure and the actual one, in money or time
the reason a variance happened: outside your control, a planning error or an execution error
what really happened, as recorded on the day, compared to what was planned

look.title: Planned Against Actual, Money (example)
look.prompt: Confirm the actual total from the planned total and the four changes, then sort each change into outside your control, a planning error or an execution error.

check.q: Chicken was planned at $2.49 per lb and cost $2.79 (example). For 4.5 lb, what is the variance?
check.why: The difference is $0.30 per lb, and $0.30 × 4.5 lb = $1.35.

check.q: The bowls were not warmed because the cook forgot, though the plan listed it. What kind of cause is this?
choices: An execution error, fixed with a checkpoint or a line on the timeline
check.why: The plan was right and was not followed. The fix is in how the plan is run, not in the plan itself.

check.q: What is the cushion on the cost sheet for?
choices: Buying a treat when the project is done
Rounding the total to a whole dollar
Covering price rises and forgotten items that are outside your control
check.why: The cushion exists so that a sale ending or a forgotten roll of foil does not break the budget.

lessons.title: What I Would Change
lessons.mainIdea: The most valuable page of the evaluation is a short, specific list of what you would do differently, each tied to a cause you found in the evidence.
reading: "What would you change?" is the question every judge, employer and teacher asks, and the weak answer is "nothing" or "everything." The strong answer is three to five specific changes, each tied to a variance and a cause. Marisol's list: cook the rice last and hold the chicken instead, because rice dries when held and chicken keeps in its resting period. Warm the bowls at the 5:30 checkpoint, written on the timeline. Buy chicken at the second store, $0.30 per lb cheaper. Put foil on every cost sheet. Add a two-person rule for clearing a course while the next one rests.

Each change has the same shape: the action, then the reason, then the evidence. Write it that way. "Start the rice at 5:25 instead of 3:20, because rice held for 79 minutes dried at the edges; see photo 14 and the texture row." A reader can check every part. A change without a reason is a guess; a change without evidence is an opinion.

Include what you would keep, too. The thermometer readings, the staged tools, the day-before dessert all worked, and a *reflection* that names the parts of the plan that held up is more useful than one that only lists faults. Then look for the change that would have prevented the most points lost. On Marisol's sheet that was the rice, which cost two points on a weight-2 row; the chicken price cost one point on the cost row. Fix the biggest one first.

Finally, write one sentence about the skill, not the dish: "I learned that holding time is part of the recipe." This is the sentence that transfers to the next project, to a job in a restaurant kitchen, to a garment shop, or to planning a family's week. The chicken is eaten; the sentence stays.

words.d: a written, honest look back at the project that names what worked, what did not and why
something learned on one project that applies to different work later
how long a finished food waits between cooking and serving

look.title: Turn Complaints Into Changes
look.text: A student's reflection reads: "The seams were kind of crooked. The bag took way longer than I thought. I ran out of thread. I should have been more careful." The documentation shows the first seam sewn without the seam guide taped on, the timeline with cutting taking 55 minutes against 20 planned, and a receipt for one spool of thread where the envelope listed two.
look.prompt: Rewrite the reflection as three changes, each with an action, a reason and the piece of evidence it comes from.

check.q: Which is the strongest answer to "What would you change?"
choices: Start the rice at 5:25 instead of 3:20, because holding it 79 minutes dried it; see the texture row and photo 14
check.why: A strong change names an action, a reason and the evidence, so a reader can check every part.

check.q: Why include what you would keep in a reflection?
choices: Because naming what worked tells you what to protect in the next plan
check.why: A reflection guides the next project; knowing which parts of the plan held up is as useful as knowing which failed.

check.q: Two changes are possible: fix the rice, which cost 4 weighted points, or fix the chicken price, which cost 2. Which is addressed first?
choices: The chicken price, because money matters most
The rice, because it cost the most points
check.why: Fix the change that would have prevented the most lost points first.

lessons.title: Presenting to an Audience
lessons.mainIdea: A project presentation walks the audience from the spec to the result to the changes in a set order, with evidence on every slide or page and the product itself in the room.
reading: Marisol's presentation was eight minutes long and had a shape. First, the spec: who the dinner was for and what it promised, one slide. Second, the plan: the menu, the cost sheet total and the timeline in one picture. Third, the production: six photos in order, from staged tools to the plated soup, with the thermometer reading on the chicken photo. Fourth, the evaluation: the rubric with her scores and her teacher's side by side. Fifth, the changes, three of them. Sixth, the lemon bars, on a tray, for the audience.

Bring the product when you can. A sewn piece is worn or held up and passed around; a dish is tasted, or shown on a plate if it cannot be. If the audience cannot taste, the photos must do the work, so use the plated photo taken in good light from above, not the one taken at the table under a yellow lamp. If someone in the audience has an allergy, say what is in the food before it is passed.

Speak from the evidence. "The chicken reached 167 °F at 5:52" is a stronger sentence than "I made sure it was cooked." "I was $2.40 over on an $85 budget (example), and here is where" is stronger than "I stayed pretty close to budget." Show the dry rice photo and say what you would change. An audience trusts a presenter who names the fault before they can find it.

Practice out loud twice, with a timer. Stand, look at the audience, and keep your hands off the slides. Expect questions, and have the cost sheet, timeline and safety page on the table to answer them. The two questions you will almost always be asked are "What was the hardest part?" and "What would you change?" You have already written both answers.

words.d: a spoken, ordered account of a project with evidence, given to an audience
the people you are presenting to, whose needs shape what you show and say
a slide, photo, table or object shown to support what you are saying

look.title: Reorder the Presentation
look.text: A student's slides are in this order: (1) final photo of the bag; (2) careers in fashion; (3) what I would change; (4) the cost sheet; (5) a photo of the crooked first seam; (6) the spec; (7) the rubric scores; (8) thank you. The bag itself is in a backpack under the desk.
look.prompt: Put the slides in the order this lesson teaches, cut any that do not belong, and say what should happen with the bag.

check.q: Which sentence belongs in a presentation?
choices: I was really careful about food safety
The chicken reached 167 °F at 5:52, recorded on the safety page
I think it was cooked enough
check.why: Presenters speak from evidence: a recorded temperature and time, not a feeling.

check.q: What is the first thing an audience should see in a project presentation?
choices: The spec: who the project was for and what it promised
check.why: The presentation follows the project's own order, and everything is judged against the spec, so the spec comes first.

check.q: Food will be passed to the audience. What must the presenter do first?
choices: Say what is in it so anyone with an allergy can decline
Pass it during the careers slide
check.why: Allergens are a safety matter for any audience, and naming the ingredients before passing food protects everyone.

lessons.title: Careers in Food and Nutrition
lessons.mainIdea: Culinary and dietetics careers use exactly the planning, costing, safety and evaluation skills of the capstone, at every level of education.
reading: Everything Marisol did for twelve people, a restaurant kitchen does for two hundred a night. A *sous chef* writes the prep list and the timeline; a purchasing manager keeps the cost sheet; a line cook holds the sauté station and reads the thermometer; a kitchen manager posts the safety page and checks the walk-in cooler is at or below 40 °F. Culinary careers range from a first job as a prep cook, often with no degree required, to executive chef, caterer, food stylist, recipe developer or restaurant owner.

Food safety itself is a career. Health inspectors visit restaurants and school cafeterias, check holding temperatures and hand-washing sinks, and write reports. Quality-assurance technicians in food plants test products and records. Many kitchen jobs require a food handler certificate, and managers often hold a food protection manager certification; both cover the same danger zone, temperatures and cross-contamination rules you posted on your safety page.

Dietetics is the science side. A registered dietitian nutritionist plans menus for hospitals, nursing homes, schools and sports teams, counsels people with diabetes or food allergies, and manages large food-service operations; the credential requires a degree, supervised practice and an exam. Dietetic technicians and nutrition assistants work alongside them. School nutrition directors plan meals for thousands of students under federal rules while meeting a budget, which is a cost sheet with more zeros.

Whatever the title, the interview questions will sound familiar. Tell me about a time you planned something under a deadline. How do you handle being over budget? What did you do when something went wrong? Your capstone is the answer: the spec, the cost sheet, the recorded temperatures, the dry rice and what you changed. Keep the documentation; it is your first portfolio.

words.d: the second-in-command in a kitchen, who runs prep lists, schedules and the line
a credentialed nutrition professional who plans menus and counsels people on food and health
a basic food-safety credential many kitchen jobs require
a collection of documented work you can show an employer or a school

look.title: Match the Task to the Job
look.text: Tasks from the capstone: writing the timeline; keeping the cost sheet; reading the thermometer and posting the temperature chart; planning a menu for a guest with a shellfish allergy; scoring the rubric. Jobs: sous chef, purchasing manager, health inspector, registered dietitian nutritionist, kitchen manager.
look.prompt: Match each task to the job that does it every day, and name one task that belongs to more than one job.

check.q: Which career plans menus for a hospital and counsels patients with diabetes?
check.why: Dietitians hold a credential based on a degree, supervised practice and an exam, and work in clinical and food-service nutrition.

check.q: A health inspector checks a restaurant's walk-in cooler. What reading passes?
check.why: Refrigeration must hold food at or below 40 °F, the bottom of the danger zone.

check.q: Why keep the capstone documentation after the course ends?
choices: In case the dinner is repeated
It is a portfolio that answers interview questions with evidence
check.why: Employers ask about planning, budgets and problems; the documented capstone shows all three.

lessons.title: Careers in Apparel, Children and Families
lessons.mainIdea: Apparel, early childhood, family services and consumer affairs careers each grow from one strand of the FCS course and use its planning and evaluation habits.
reading: The student who sewed the tote bag from a spec did in miniature what an apparel industry does at scale. A *patternmaker* turns a designer's sketch into the pattern pieces with grainlines and notches; a technical designer writes the spec sheet with every finished measurement and seam finish; a sample sewer makes the first one; a quality inspector measures it against the spec with a tape and a seam gauge. Related jobs include tailor, alterations specialist, costume technician for theater, textile buyer and merchandiser, and the sustainability roles now growing as companies try to cut textile waste.

Early childhood careers build on the child development strand. Preschool and child-care teachers plan a day around routines, choices and redirection; Head Start and early-intervention staff work with families of children with disabilities; a child-care center director manages safety plans, ratios, budgets and menus all at once. Most states require training hours and a background check for child-care work, and many roles require an associate or bachelor's degree. The safe-sleep rules and choking-hazard lists from your course are posted in every infant room.

Family and community services and consumer affairs are the strand that helps households manage. Family support workers, case managers and Extension educators teach budgeting, meal planning and parenting in community settings; the University of Illinois Extension runs nutrition and family programs across the state. Consumer affairs roles include credit counselors, housing counselors, and staff at agencies that handle complaints and scams. Financial literacy teachers and FCS teachers themselves are in this group, and there is a shortage of them in many districts.

Look across all of these and notice what repeats: a plan written before the work, a cost sheet, a safety page, evidence gathered as you go, an honest evaluation and a clear report. That is the capstone, and it is also a description of nearly any job worth having. Choose a strand that interests you, find one person who works in it, and ask them the question you have learned to answer: what would you change?

words.d: the apparel worker who turns a design into pattern pieces with grainlines, notches and seam allowances
services for infants and toddlers with developmental delays or disabilities and their families
a university-based teacher who brings nutrition, family and money programs to communities
work that protects and informs buyers: complaints, credit and housing counseling, scam prevention

look.title: One Skill, Five Jobs
look.text: The capstone skill: write a measurable spec and then evaluate the result against it. Five workplaces: a garment factory's quality station; an infant room at a child-care center; a credit counseling office; a school cafeteria kitchen; a theater costume shop.
look.prompt: For each workplace, describe what the spec would contain and what tool or record would be used to check the result against it.

check.q: Which job writes the spec sheet with every finished measurement and seam finish for a garment?
check.why: The technical designer's spec sheet is the industry version of the capstone specification.

check.q: Which rule from the child development strand is posted in every licensed infant room?
choices: Infants sleep on their stomach to prevent spit-up
Infants sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface with nothing else in the crib
Infants sleep with a soft blanket for warmth
Infants nap in a car seat
check.why: Safe sleep is on the back, on a firm flat surface, with nothing else in the crib.

check.q: What does nearly every FCS career have in common with the capstone?
choices: A college degree in the same subject
A plan, a cost sheet, a safety rule set, evidence, evaluation and a report
check.why: The capstone's cycle of plan, cost, produce, document, evaluate and present is the shape of the work in every strand.

review.q: At a checkpoint you are 20 minutes behind. Which may never be cut to catch up?
choices: The thermometer reading on the chicken
review.why: Nothing on the safety page is ever cut; garnishes and extras go first.

review.q: Which is evidence that a dish met the safety plan?
choices: A written internal temperature with the time it was read
A photo of the browned crust
A guest saying it tasted done
review.why: Only a recorded thermometer reading proves the safe minimum internal temperature was reached.

review.q: Hot soup must wait 45 minutes before serving. What temperature must it be held above?
review.why: Hot food is held above 140 °F, the top of the danger zone, until served.

review.q: A cost sheet planned $85 and receipts total $87.40 (example). What is the most useful next step?
choices: Compare line by line to find which items caused the variance and why
review.why: The lines, not the total, show the causes, and the causes are what get fixed next time.

review.q: The plan listed warming the bowls and the cook forgot. What kind of cause is this?
review.why: The plan was right and was not followed; the fix is a checkpoint or a timeline line that catches it.

review.q: Which is the strongest "what I would change" statement?
choices: Start the rice at 5:25, because holding it 79 minutes dried it, as photo 14 and the texture row show
review.why: Action, reason and evidence together make a change a reader can check.

review.q: In what order should a project presentation run?
choices: Spec, plan, production, evaluation, changes, product
Product, then whatever the audience asks
review.why: The presentation follows the project's own order, from the spec everything is judged against to the finished product.

review.q: Which credential plans hospital menus and counsels patients on nutrition?
review.why: The registered dietitian nutritionist credential requires a degree, supervised practice and an exam.
